noi_dung:
Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva Is Our Elder Brother

Every day we recite the name of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, but what does "Avalokiteshvara" mean? "Avalokita" means contemplating the sounds of the world. "Avalokita" also means looking—not looking outward, but looking into the minds of living beings, to see whose mind is free of scattered discursive thoughts. With no more discursive thoughts and the mind empty, that is enlightenment. Hence it is said:

"Gathered together from the ten directions,

We study together the Dharma of non-action."

Reciting the name of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva is also a dharma of non-action. "Non-action" means doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone—that is, it teaches us not to give rise to discursive thoughts.

When you recite "Nam Mô Quán Thế Âm Bồ-tát", Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva also recites you—the two sides recite each other, just as when you fondly remember your kin, your kin also remember you. We and Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva have, from limitless kalpas past until now, been kin in the Dharma, relatives in the Buddhadharma. Kin since when? Counting from the time of Amitabha Buddha! Amitabha Buddha is the Teaching Host of the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West, and he is also the teacher of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva helps Amitabha propagate the Pure Land Dharma-door. We are none other than fellow disciples of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva is the eldest brother to all living beings who have not yet been reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so living beings are his younger siblings. Put that way, it is clear that he and we are very close kin. Therefore, whenever we remember our elder brother, our elder brother also remembers us. We are Avalokiteshvara's younger siblings, and Avalokiteshvara is our elder brother.

Someone says: "How can Avalokiteshvara possibly be my elder brother? Isn't that going too far?" Not only does Avalokiteshvara regard us as younger siblings, he regards all living beings as his youngest siblings besides. If it were not so, why would he contemplate sounds and rescue the suffering? Why is it that whenever living beings meet with difficulty, he comes to their rescue? It is because he regards living beings as his own flesh and blood that he fears no hardship and goes to rescue all suffering beings in this Saha world. Therefore, do not forget your elder brother in the Dharma—each time we recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva at once fondly remembers us.

When we recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, it is we who are calling out to our elder brother. When Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva calls our names, it is he who is calling his younger siblings—that is, the Bodhisattvas of the future, the Buddhas of the future.

Seeing Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva in this way, we must all the more recite the name of our own brother in the Dharma with sincerity and earnestness, and not let this opportunity slip by. When reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, do not hang your head down; hold your head up, expressing a valiant and vigorous spirit. Do not look droopy and drowsy. When Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva sees your vigorous spirit, he will say to you: "Quickly take my hand!" And then he will lead you to the world of Ultimate Bliss.

Someone idly wonders: "Why is it that Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva just looks and looks from morning to night, while I am not allowed to look at anything?" Your "looking" and Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's "looking" are very different! Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva looks inward, while you look outward. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva contemplates his own nature. His mind-nature is like a radar screen on which all living beings appear. Whatever discursive thoughts living beings have, he knows them all. He looks at the radar screen within, unlike the way you look. Because living beings are so far from him, even with a thousand hands and a thousand eyes, to look upon limitless beings would still not be enough hands, not enough eyes. Therefore he returns the light and reflects it inward, and turns the hearing around to listen to his own nature. He contemplates the own-nature of living beings to see who is suffering, and then he goes to rescue them. But you look outward, forgetting your own fundamental wisdom. Hence your looking and his looking are completely different.

Someone else thinks: "Master! I don't believe what you teach! Why don't I believe it? Because you say we are siblings with Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, yet he is a sage and we are common beings; how can common beings be siblings with a sage? That is unreasonable, so I don't believe it." Very good! You may disbelieve; what you say has its logic. But that logic belongs to the knowledge and views of common beings, for you have not deeply entered the Sutra Treasury and so lack wisdom as vast and deep as the sea.

The Avatamsaka Sutra teaches: "The Bodhisattva reflects thus: From beginningless kalpas past until now, I and living beings have been brothers, parents, sisters, husbands and wives to one another." That you say you do not believe is simply because you do not clearly understand the principle taught in the Avatamsaka Sutra.

Moreover, not only does the Bodhisattva see living beings this way—even the Buddha regards living beings as "all men are my fathers, all women are my mothers." If the Buddha regards living beings as his parents, then what is unreasonable about my saying that Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva regards living beings as his siblings? That you say you do not believe is just because you lack wisdom and knowledge. Or perhaps your view is too narrow, and so you have become deluded and disbelieve what I say.

Why does the Buddha wish to save living beings? Because he holds that "all men are my fathers, all women are my mothers." Since his fathers and mothers are suffering in the cycle of the six paths of rebirth, no matter what, he must rescue them and enable them to leave suffering and attain bliss.

Every day we recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, we bow to Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva; yet when he appears before us, we do not recognize him. So we living beings are truly pitiful! Why is it that Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva appears before us and we do not know it? This is a test for us. When you recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, you must learn to become like him. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva has great kindness, great compassion, great vows, and great power; therefore, when reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, we must learn to have great kindness, great compassion, great vows, and great power—if anyone treats us badly, let our minds be unmoved; if anyone scolds us, we must bear it in silence; if anyone beats us, we must endure it; and even if someone kills us, we must accept it, taking it as repayment of a debt! What is "repaying a debt"? For example, had we never scolded anyone in the past, no one would scold us now; had we never beaten anyone, no one would beat us now. Why is it that someone comes to scold, beat, or even kill us? Because in the past, when we were deluded, we scolded, beat, and killed others; therefore in this life we must settle those old debts in full. In the past, deluded, we owed debts and did not repay them. Today, understanding the Way, we must sincerely repay those debts in full. Once we have repaid all our debts, we will see Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and become his kin in the Dharma.

So, having recited Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, whomever we meet, we must not go looking for their faults. If we keep picking at others' faults, our own suffering is not yet ended, and we have not yet cut off suffering at its root. Therefore, clearly recognize every state you meet, and penetrate to the root of every matter. In studying the Buddhadharma, you must know how to apply the Buddhadharma. If you do not know how to apply it, then no matter how long you cultivate, the Buddhadharma remains the Buddhadharma, and you remain you. When you know how to apply it, you merge into one with the Buddhadharma, with nothing separating you.

Patience is the most essential dharma. You must be able to endure what is hard to endure. For example, you dislike being scolded, yet when someone scolds you, gladly endure it. Though you dislike being beaten, when someone beats you, gladly bear it. You do not want to die, for human life is precious; yet if someone wants to kill you, regard them as liberating you from a lifetime of karmic obstacles—they are truly a Good Knowing Advisor. Friends! In studying the Buddhadharma, we must turn our attitude around and study; in cultivating the Way, we must turn our attitude around and cultivate! What does turning our attitude around mean? It means gladly doing what we formerly disliked doing, and never imposing on others what we ourselves dislike.

If you are just like ordinary people: unable to see through, unable to let go, unable to cut off attachment to "self" and to "dharmas," tightly holding the four discriminating views of self, others, living beings, and a life—then you will have endless trouble and vexation. If you know how to take a step back, everything naturally becomes calm, like a still sea and a clear sky. In studying the Buddhadharma, do not chase after what is lofty and recondite, for:

"The ordinary mind is the Way,

The straightforward mind is the Way-place."

(The ordinary mind—the mind without desires—is the Way;

The straightforward heart is the Way-place, the place of cultivation.)

That is why in cultivation we need an upright and straightforward heart.

When reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, do not be greedy. Do not think: "If I recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, I'll get rich!" That can never be! When you are free of greed, wealth may come; once greed arises, you will gain nothing. When reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, do not show off: "I've been here and there to join Avalokiteshvara Sessions. You've never joined one, so you're not my equal!" Do not give rise to such discursive thoughts, and do not crave fame, gain, or comfortable enjoyment.

When reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, recite in an ordinary way; do not seek after anything. Do not imitate those who recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva while thinking: "I am childless; I pray Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva will give me a son." Some pray for a daughter; many young men recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva praying for a pretty girlfriend, and many young women recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva praying to meet a boyfriend—none of these can be had that way! When reciting Avalokiteshvara's name, sweep all such impure thoughts away. Do not harbor greed, anger, or delusion. For instance, when you put on clothes each day, do not mind whether they are fine or not—warmth is enough. When you eat each day, do not crave delicacies. If you harbor such thoughts, you are no longer reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva with a true mind. If you sincerely recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, why would you still think of fine food and fine clothes? You should have forgotten all those things long ago! There is only one way: forget everything, and then we can merge into one with Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva.

Within the mind of every living being there is already an Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva. Right now, as we recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, we are reciting the Avalokiteshvara within our own minds. Someone says: "I look into my mind, but I can't find my mind anywhere!" If you had no mind, you wouldn't need to recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva at all. For that very absence (your having no mind to find) is Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva is precisely the absence of mind, because he never gives rise to discursive thoughts, nor has greed, anger, or delusion. He never schemes over what fine clothes to wear today, what delicious dish to eat, or what offerings to enjoy. He is attached to nothing and seeks nothing. What he does is rescue living beings, vowing that all beings may leave suffering and attain bliss, end birth and death, and accomplish the Buddha Way. He seeks nothing from living beings. He hopes living beings can truly understand the Buddhadharma and completely rid themselves of greed, anger, and delusion.

When reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, do not chatter idly all day: "No breakfast in the morning, no tea at night—this is too miserable! I can't stand it anymore; quickly pack up and run!" Cultivating that way is utterly worthless!

(Explained on March 16, 1976)
